newsitem.title: POLAND: No profit seen in new Polish money market status.
newsitem.headline: No profit seen in new Polish money market status.

text.p: The status of money market dealer, awarded to 17 Polish banks by the National Bank of Poland (NBP) this year, is purely prestigious and unlikely to yield significant profit on commissions, dealers said.
The 17 banks, out of Poland's more than 80, have exclusive access to the central bank's open market operations -- repos, reverse repos, NBP-bill auctions and outright T-bill sales.
Dealers said commissions from charging non-dealers for participation in NBP operations were meagre because of fierce competition among the dealer banks.

"There is no big money in it, but the situation on the market is more clear now and it was a step in the right direction," said Adam Gadomski of Bank Handlowy, which retained its dealer status from last year.
"High competition among dealer banks is likely to cut the already low commissions," said Gracjan Grzymkowski, chief dealer at BGZ SA, a bank which lost the privilege.

Traders said individually negotiated commissions charged by dealer banks for placing non-dealer funds at NBP reverse repos were between 0.01 to 0.05 percent of the placed sum and barely covered the costs of the operation.

Some dealers said the costs of getting the dealer status were fairly high as competing banks had cut prices of T-bills offered to customers in 1996 to meet central bank turnover and client portfolio-size criteria.
"The money market dealer certificate cost us real money," said a dealer at a major Polish bank which retained its dealership.

Competition for the status almost doubled the turnover in secondary T-bill trade, one of the central bank criteria, to 51.8 billion zlotys since the July 1996 start of the evaluation period, central bank figures showed.
Trade in NBP-bills rocketed to 17 billion zlotys in November from July's 512 million, the data showed.
The average daily amount of T-bills in portfolios of domestic non-banking institutions, the most important criterion, rose to nine billion zlotys in November from 6.37 billion zlotys in July.
Some large banks which lost the status in 1997 also said they did not have credit limits big enough for some of the new dealers to use them to place funds with the NBP.
